lines.note: Tsuzukete continues the preceding page's example of working continuously; the Portuguese specifies diligence without stopping. The divided des- belongs to descansar below.
Completes the explanation as neither resting nor interrupting the task. The following Tçu- starts a new example, not a new headword.
Together with Tçu- above, tsumetsukete yuu describes speaking insistently, with kou supplied as the alternative for asking. The printed attached form metçuqeteyǔ and its vowel marks are retained.
Completes dizer ou pedir as speaking or asking importunately and without intervals. Interpolação here concerns interruption or intervening time.
Tsumeotoshi, tsumeotosu, tsumeotoita means compelling a position to surrender. The historical -oita principal part is supported by the remaining type; porforça retains the printed close spacing.

Shiro wo tsumeotosu means taking a fortress by pressing it to surrender. The damaged Xirouo and tçumevotoſu fit the visible letters and the explicit fortress gloss, unlike OCR Xitouo and tçamevotoſu; Tomar is entirely italic.
Fortaleza por força completes the preceding Portuguese phrase: taking a fortress by force. The capital F belongs to the printed continuation.
Tsumeyose denotes pressing forward or bringing others close by force. The noun força has f, not the OCR's long s, as the visible cross-stroke and meaning both support.

runs.text: fazer chegar como à fortaleza, ou aos inimi-

lines.note: The gloss includes causing an approach to a fortress or to enemies. The divided inimi- continues into inimigos below; its printed hyphen remains.
Completes inimigos and closes the examples of approaching hostile positions. This short continuation is a separate physical row.
Tsumi, alternatively tsumu, is a spindle for spinning silk or cotton. The scan's algodão corrects OCR algadão without modernizing the other historical spellings.
Tsumi de ito wo tsumugu illustrates spinning thread with the spindle. Torcer begins the Portuguese explanation and is italic throughout, including its capital T.

runs.text: fio, ou fiado, & ajuntalo no fuſo.

lines.note: Completes torcer as twisting thread or spun material and collecting it on the spindle. The narrow i is visible in fiado; OCR fado would lose part of the word.
Tsumi first means sin, then punishment or penalty. Peccado visibly has doubled c here, although the same entry later also uses single-c pecado.
The penalty is for sin. Tsumi wo nadamuru introduces pardoning an offence or remitting its punishment, with Portuguese perdoar divided across the row boundary.

runs.text: doar o crime, ou pena por elle merecida.

lines.note: Completes perdoar: pardon the crime or the punishment deserved for it. This keeps the two objects of the remission distinct.
Tsumi wo itou means rejecting or detesting sin. The circumflex in itô is retained, and aborre- begins the Portuguese verb continued below.
After completing aborrecer o peccado, the example tsumi wo horobosu means destroying or eliminating sin. The damaged object particle is uo, not OCR to; the Portuguese desfazer begins at the end.
Completes desfazer and adds destruir, both describing elimination of sin. The next divided form Tçumi- begins the passive expression on the following line; single-c pecado is retained here.
Tsumi-seraruru is the passive construction for being punished or subjected to justice. The middle letters are abraded, but the remaining shapes and the Portuguese support the supplied xeraruru.

runs.text: algum crime Commummente eſtes modos de

lines.note: The punishment is for a crime, after which the dictionary comments on the register of these expressions. No punctuation is supplied between crime and Commummente where the scan does not securely show it.
Completes the register comment: these ways of speaking are commonly used in books. The statement applies to the preceding sin and punishment expressions.
Tsumi, tsumu, tsunda is the verb for piling up or stowing. It is distinct from the preceding noun tsumi, sin, despite the same headword spelling.
Fune ni ni wo tsumu means loading cargo onto a vessel. The scan supports niuo, with ni denoting the cargo; OCR miuo obscured the object. Fato here means baggage or goods.
Naembarcação completes the cargo-stowing example. Kou wo tsumu introduces accumulating practice or merit, glossed here as forming a habit; the close printed naembarcação is retained.

Ienno is interpreted as zen no in the example of accumulating merit in virtue. The damaged middle of Ienno is read from the surviving strokes and this context; the reading remains less secure than the clearly printed côuo tçumu.

Completes the habit-in-virtue gloss, then illustrates snow piling up as it falls. The print has a gap before çumu without a secure t; furi çumu is retained rather than silently supplying the expected furitçumu.

Tsumoru is offered as an alternative in the snow example. The Portuguese says that much falls and the snow increases; Chouer is retained even though the example concerns snow rather than ordinary rain.
Completes neve em montes: snow accumulating in heaps. This is the short final continuation of the accumulation verb's examples.
This tsumi, tsumu, tsunda means plucking or gathering by hand, with herbs, leaves, and roses as examples. It is a separate lexical entry from piling up.
The gloss finishes with gathering by hand. Shii wo tsumu then describes removing and eating the kernel of an acorn-like fruit, with esbrugar divided across the line break.

runs.text: gar com os dentes, & comer esta fruita que

lines.note: Completes esbrugar as stripping or opening with the teeth and eating the fruit. The following relative clause identifies the fruit by comparison.

runs.text: he como bolotas: o meſmo ſe dirà de outra frui

lines.note: The fruit resembles acorns, and the same expression can apply to another similar fruit. Frui continues into fruta below without adding an unprinted terminal hyphen.

runs.text: ta ſemelhante, ou de eſpiga darroz, &c.

lines.note: Completes fruta semelhante and adds a rice ear as another possible object. The printed contraction darroz is preserved rather than expanded.
Mame nado wo tsumu means eating beans or similar seeds by biting them apart. The comma after Mame is part of the printed example rather than an editorial segmentation.

runs.text: ou outro legume partindoo com os dentes.

lines.note: Completes the example as eating another legume by breaking it with the teeth. The attached object form partindoo is retained.
Wata wo tsumu illustrates opening or teasing out fibre with the fingers. Vatauo is the printed form of the Japanese object phrase.
Completes the fibre-working gloss as teasing out floss or cotton. The Portuguese distinguishes the materials borra and algodão without requiring a modern botanical identification.
Tsumiage describes piling up in quantity. The printed principal forms are retained, with the Portuguese explanation continued below.
The gloss specifies gathering as if into heaps. The citation begins with ryoora and kinshu, costly silk fabrics and brocades, whose accumulation is described in the following rows.

The quotation describes treasures including those fabrics being piled like mountains. Both circumflexes in chôfôuo are visible; the first was omitted by OCR. Tçumi continues into aguete without an added hyphen.
Aguete completes tsumiagete. Taif. is the printed citation label, followed by the italic book reference and the Portuguese translation beginning with gathering together.

runs.text: como montes de vestidos ricos, & outras peças

lines.note: The translation describes heaps of rich garments and other valuable objects. The physical line ends at peças, with its qualification on the next row.
Completes the valuable-object phrase and adds riches as the alternative description. It closes the quotation rather than introducing another headword.
Tsumikasane means piling things repeatedly or in layers. The damaged middle of the headword is supported by its remaining types and the following explanation of placing things on others.

runs.text: ou por huas couſas ſobre outras.

lines.note: Completes the definition as placing some things on top of others. The small word is abraded: huas is chosen from the surviving letters without supplying an unestablished tilde.

Tsumogori is glossed as the last day of the month. The scan's unusual consonant order is preserved, not changed to the familiar tsugomori; the supplied NINJAL headword index independently corroborates Tçumogori.

zones.label: Column 2 running header
zones.note: The right running header prints DA, unlike DO in the left header.

lines.note: Tsumori, tsumoru, tsumotta denotes increasing or accumulating intransitively. The Portuguese acumularse is divided across the physical row boundary.
Completes acumularse, then begins the comparison: accumulated water becomes a deep pool. Mizzu is the historical spelling of mizu, and fuchito belongs to the resulting state.
The second half compares accumulated learning with becoming a sage or learned person. Xix. is the printed source label; the Portuguese translation begins with Aßi at the right edge.

runs.text: como a agoa crecendo ſe faz hum pègo fundo,

lines.note: The Portuguese restates the first half: water increasing makes a deep pool. Pègo retains its printed grave accent and historical sense of a deep body of water.

runs.text: aßi com o estudo ſe faz hum grande letrado.

lines.note: Completes the comparison: study makes a great scholar. The low-s construction in estudo is retained as supplied rather than changed by a blanket long-s rule.
Toshi, tsuki, hi ga tsumoru illustrates years, months, and days accumulating. The Portuguese verb acrecentar begins at the end of the row.
Completes the explanation as years, months, and days increasing. Dias is visible rather than OCR duas; Fica- begins the Japanese hikazu example below.
Joined with Fica-, hikazu ga tsumoru means that the number of days accumulates. The Portuguese expresses many days passing; the printed attached zugatçumoru remains unsegmented.
Toga or tsumi accumulating means offences or sins mounting up. The scan clearly gives initial T and a preceding paragraph sign, correcting OCR Foga and its missing marker.
Completes the accumulation-of-sins gloss. Zai- begins the next example about wealth, with zaifoo divided across this row and the next.
Together with Zai-, zaifoo ga tsumoru means riches increasing. The visible circumflex is retained in the second part of the divided word.
Chiri tsumotte yama to naru is the image of accumulated dust becoming a mountain. The Portuguese begins its explanation of small accumulated things producing something large.

runs.text: nas couſas acumuladas ſe fazem grandes.

lines.note: Completes pequenas and the proverbial explanation: great things are made from small things accumulated. This closes the intransitive verb's examples.
The noun tsumori is glossed as a collection, compilation, or sum. It is kept distinct from the preceding inflected verb entry.

runs.text: Fuſo de ferro pera fiar ſe-

lines.note: Tsumu, alternatively tsumi, is an iron spindle for spinning. The silk reference is divided at ſe- and continues below; this is the counterpart of the spindle entry in column 1.
Completes seda and lists cotton and other materials spun with the spindle. The short continuation is retained as its own physical line.

runs.text: Peças tecidas com borra de Iapão.

lines.note: Tsumugi names cloth woven from the fibre or floss called borra in the Portuguese explanation. Iapão is Portuguese for Japan and remains part of the italic gloss.
The verb tsumugi, tsumugu, tsumuida means twisting or spinning thread. The principal part uida is the historical inflection, and re- begins the Portuguese material term below.
Completes retros and adds the sense of spinning. Wata or ito is the object of the Japanese example, whose verb is divided tçu-mugu; Itẽ preserves the printed abbreviation.
Completes tsumugu, with the Portuguese specifying spinning floss or silk. The line closes the example rather than starting a new headword.
Tsuna is a hawser or thick rope, directly matched by amarra and corda grossa. The two long-s forms in groſſa are retained as supplied.
Tsunade, alternatively tsunate, denotes a vessel's ropes or hawsers. The qualifying ship word appears on the next row.
Da Fune completes the Portuguese phrase with the embedded Japanese fune, boat. Fune is visibly within the Portuguese explanation and is recorded as a whole-word typeface term.
Tsunagi, tsunagu, tsunaida means tying or mooring. The explanation begins with animals as objects of the action and continues with a vessel below.
Embarcação completes the objects that may be tied or moored. This brief row belongs to the preceding verb's explanation.
Tsunagibashira denotes posts for tying animals. The scan has gui before baxira, restoring the OCR's omitted i; the supplied NINJAL index also records this headword.
Completes the definition as posts to which animals are tied in the stable. Bestas here refers to beasts or mounts, not a separate lexical item.
Tsunate is again defined as a vessel's ropes or hawsers. This independent entry gives the alternative previously cited under tsunade.
Tsunena and tsuneno qualify something as common or usual. The damaged capital has the T form seen in adjacent headwords, not the OCR's r.
Ordinaria completes the adjective gloss, ordinary or customary. It is a separate short continuation of the preceding pair of forms.
Tsuneni is the adverb meaning always or commonly. Adu. and the entire Portuguese apparatus are italic; both visible abbreviation tildes in cõmũmente are retained.
Tsuneshiki no describes something customary or ordinary. The xe spelling is regular Jesuit notation and does not call for modernization to se.
Tsunezune is explained as always or many times. The doubled zz belongs to the printed form, while the frequency gloss continues below.
Vezes completes muitas vezes, many times. This single-word line finishes the adverb's explanation.
Tsunmawashi is an equestrian term for making a horse turn while pulling it. The line ends with pu-, not OCR ou-, and the next row completes puxãdo.

runs.text: xãdo pera aparte eſquerda o meſmo caualo.

lines.note: Completes puxãdo and specifies pulling the horse toward the left side. Fin starts the contrasting term on the next row; the apparent directional inconsistency in that contrast is preserved and discussed below.

runs.text: He o contrario. ſ. da parte direi-

lines.note: Finmauaxi is said to be the contrary, followed by the visible explanatory abbreviation ſ. and a direction beginning at the right side. The Japanese term is divided across rows; it is not marked as separate typeface fragments.

Completes direita pera a esquerda, from right to left. The print repeats esquerda despite describing the contrary of the preceding leftward action; this internal inconsistency is retained without changing the directions.

Tsuno means horn; the example is glossed as an animal's horns emerging. The printed vowel sequence vouoru is retained rather than reconstructed as a familiar modern verb form, and the capital T corrects OCR ſ.
Completes nacerem cornos ao animal, horns growing on the animal. The scan has cerem followed by cornos, without the extra s produced by OCR.

runs.text: Certo vaſo como gamela cõ hũas

lines.note: Tsunodarai is a vessel resembling a shallow tub and having projecting points. The Portuguese description continues below, explaining its use for washing hands.

runs.text: pontas ſaidas pera fora cõ q̃ ſe da agoa às mãos.

lines.note: The projections extend outward, and the vessel supplies water to the hands. The abbreviated cõ and q̃ are preserved without expansion.

runs.text: Frecha que tem corno por ferro.

lines.note: Tsunogi is an arrow using horn in place of an iron point. The initial capital T is clear in the same type as nearby headwords, correcting OCR ſ.
Tsunogumi, tsunogumu, tsunogunda describes shoots beginning to sprout. The Portuguese gives brotar and nacer as alternatives, with the plants specified below.

runs.text: caninhas nouas, ou caniços das alagoas. Vt,

lines.note: The shoots are new little canes or reeds of marshes and pools. Italic Vt introduces the Japanese reed example on the following line.
Ashi no tsunogumu illustrates reeds putting out young shoots. This standalone Japanese example remains roman and is not treated as words embedded in a Portuguese sentence.
Tsunori, tsunoru, tsunotta means increasing or becoming stronger. Crecer restores the scan's capital C, and the explanation continues on the next page; the separate fazerſe catchword is furniture.
Anticipates fazerſe at the opening of f0488; retained under its original stable ID as page furniture, not counted again as body text.
